title: Inside the GPU: A Complete Guide for AI and Machine Learning Engineers
partialText:
A practical technical guide for Machine Learning Engineers, Deep Learning Engineers, AI Architects and GenAI practitioners

Introduction: Why every AI engineer needs to understand GPUs

Artificial Intelligence has entered an era where computational power is becoming just as important as algorithmic innovation.

From training Large Language Models (LLMs) and running transformer architectures to building autonomous AI agents, multimodal systems, diffusion models and real-time inference pipelines, GPUs have become the backbone of modern AI infrastructure.

Consider a few familiar activities:

  • Training a neural network on millions of images.
  • Fine-tuning an open-source LLM using LoRA or QLoRA.
  • Generating responses from a 70-billion-parameter language model.
  • Running multiple AI agents simultaneously.
  • Serving thousands of concurrent inference requests.

All these workloads depend heavily on how efficiently mathematical operations are executed on hardware.

But here is an important distinction:

A GPU is not simply a faster CPU. It is a fundamentally different computing architecture designed to execute massive numbers of mathematical operations in parallel.

For AI engineers, understanding GPUs means understanding much more than CUDA programming. It means knowing how computation, memory bandwidth, tensor operations, precision, parallelism and hardware architecture interact to determine the performance and cost of an AI system.

This article builds that understanding from the ground up.

What exactly is a GPU?

A Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is a specialized processor originally designed to accelerate graphics rendering.

Rendering a 3D scene involves calculating the color, lighting, texture and position of millions of pixels. Many of these calculations can be performed independently.

This makes graphics workloads naturally parallel.

Researchers and engineers eventually recognized that the same computational structure appears in machine learning.

For example, consider matrix multiplication:

This operation is fundamental to neural networks, transformers, attention mechanisms and many other AI algorithms.

A CPU can perform these operations efficiently, but a GPU can distribute thousands of smaller computations across its processing units.

That makes GPUs particularly effective for workloads involving large-scale parallel mathematical operations.

CPU vs GPU: The architectural difference

CPU

Designed for latency and general-purpose computing.

  • Few powerful cores
  • Complex control logic
  • Large caches
  • Strong sequential performance

GPU

Designed for throughput and parallel computing.

  • Many processing units
  • Massive parallelism
  • High memory bandwidth
  • Specialized matrix hardware

The distinction is not that CPUs are incapable of AI computation. Rather, GPUs are architecturally optimized for the kinds of operations that dominate deep learning.

Inside a GPU: Understanding its architecture

To understand why GPUs are so effective at AI workloads, we need to look inside the processor.

A modern data-center GPU contains several interconnected components:

  1. Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs).
  2. CUDA cores or equivalent general-purpose processing units.
  3. Tensor Cores or specialized matrix-processing units.
  4. Registers and shared memory.
  5. L1 and L2 caches.
  6. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).
  7. Memory controllers and high-speed interconnects.

Let’s understand each component.

Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)

On NVIDIA GPUs, the Streaming Multiprocessor is one of the fundamental execution units.

Think of an SM as a small processing department inside a massive computing factory.

Each SM contains:

  • CUDA cores for general arithmetic operations.
  • Tensor Cores for accelerated matrix operations.
  • Registers for fast temporary storage.
  • Shared memory for communication between threads.
  • Scheduling hardware to manage execution.

A GPU contains multiple SMs, and each SM executes thousands of lightweight threads over time.

For example, NVIDIA’s H100 architecture contains 132 Streaming Multiprocessors. The exact configuration varies across GPU models and variants.

CUDA Cores

CUDA cores are NVIDIA’s general-purpose GPU arithmetic execution units.

They execute operations such as:

  • Addition and multiplication.
  • Floating-point calculations.
  • Integer arithmetic.
  • Other operations required by parallel workloads.

In deep learning, CUDA cores can execute general mathematical operations, but matrix multiplication is increasingly accelerated through specialized Tensor Cores.

Important: CUDA cores are not equivalent to CPU cores. Comparing their counts directly is misleading because the underlying architectures and execution models are different.

Tensor Cores: The real AI acceleration engine

Tensor Cores are specialized hardware units designed to accelerate matrix multiplication and multiply-accumulate operations.

Consider a neural network layer:

Where:

  • X = input matrix
  • W = weight matrix
  • b = bias
  • Y = output matrix

The matrix multiplication XW is computationally expensive, especially when the matrices contain millions or billions of elements.

Tensor Cores accelerate these operations by performing many multiply-accumulate calculations simultaneously.

This is particularly important for:

  • Transformer attention.
  • Feed-forward neural networks.
  • Convolutional neural networks.
  • LLM training.
  • LLM inference.

For AI engineers, one important lesson is that using a GPU does not automatically mean your code is taking full advantage of Tensor Cores.

Your data types, tensor shapes, library implementations and hardware generation all influence whether specialized acceleration is being utilized.

GPU memory hierarchy: Why memory matters as much as compute

This is probably the most important concept for engineers working with modern LLMs.

A GPU can have enormous computational capability, but it cannot perform efficiently if it cannot access data quickly enough.

This is known as the memory bottleneck.

A GPU has multiple levels of memory, each with different capacity, speed and accessibility.

Understanding the memory hierarchy

The hierarchy is important because moving data between memory levels has a cost.

For example, imagine a matrix multiplication operation:

If every thread repeatedly fetches values from global GPU memory, the operation may become memory-bound.

An optimized implementation loads data into shared memory, reuses it across multiple calculations and reduces expensive memory transfers.

This technique is called tiling.

What is VRAM?

VRAM, or Video Random Access Memory, is the GPU’s dedicated memory.

In data-center AI accelerators, this is commonly implemented using High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

VRAM stores:

  • Model parameters.
  • Input and output tensors.
  • Gradients.
  • Optimizer states.
  • Intermediate activations.
  • Attention KV caches.
  • Temporary computation buffers.

The amount of VRAM determines how large a model or workload can fit on a GPU, while memory bandwidth determines how quickly data can be transferred.

These are two different properties.

Memory capacity answers: Can I fit the model?

Memory bandwidth answers: How quickly can I feed the GPU with data?

The difference becomes important when running LLM inference.

For example, autoregressive generation repeatedly reads model weights to generate the next token. When inference is memory-bound, higher memory bandwidth can significantly improve throughput.

GPU memory capacity

Why GPU memory is critical for LLMs

Let’s take a hypothetical 70-billion-parameter language model.

If every parameter is stored using 16-bit precision:

This means the model weights alone require approximately 140 GB.

But the actual memory requirement is higher because inference also needs:

  • KV cache.
  • Runtime workspace.
  • Temporary tensors.
  • CUDA context and framework allocations.

A GPU with 80 GB VRAM cannot hold this entire model in FP16 without partitioning, quantization or offloading.

This is why AI infrastructure decisions cannot be based only on GPU compute performance.

Understanding GPU parallelism: Threads, Warps and Blocks

One of the biggest differences between CPU and GPU programming is the execution model.

In CPU programming, we typically think in terms of processes and threads.

In CUDA programming, NVIDIA uses a hierarchical execution model:

Let’s use a simple example.

Suppose you want to add two arrays containing one million numbers:

Each output element can be calculated independently.

A GPU can distribute these calculations across thousands of threads.

Conceptually:

  • Thread 1 calculates element 1.
  • Thread 2 calculates element 2.
  • Thread 3 calculates element 3.
  • Thousands of other threads calculate other elements.

The GPU schedules these threads across its SMs.

This is called Single Instruction, Multiple Threads (SIMT).

Why does this matter to AI engineers?

Neural networks contain enormous numbers of independent mathematical operations.

For example, a matrix multiplication involving large matrices can be divided into smaller tiles and distributed across multiple thread blocks.

This is one reason GPUs are so effective for deep learning.

However, parallelism also introduces challenges:

  • Thread synchronization.
  • Memory contention.
  • Load imbalance.
  • Branch divergence.
  • Kernel launch overhead.

An important GPU optimization principle is to keep computational units busy while minimizing unnecessary synchronization and memory movement.

Floating-point precision: FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4

AI engineers frequently encounter different numerical precision formats.

Why?

Because using 32-bit floating-point numbers for every operation is not always necessary.

Modern GPUs contain specialized hardware that can execute lower-precision operations much faster and with less memory consumption.

Let’s understand the formats.

Why BF16 is important

BF16 stands for Brain Floating Point 16.

It uses:

  • 1 sign bit.
  • 8 exponent bits.
  • 7 fraction bits.

FP16 uses:

  • 1 sign bit.
  • 5 exponent bits.
  • 10 fraction bits.

The important difference is that BF16 retains the same exponent width as FP32.

This gives BF16 a much wider numerical range than FP16, which can be beneficial when training large neural networks.

Mixed precision training

Mixed precision training combines different numerical formats to improve performance without sacrificing too much numerical accuracy.

For example:

  1. Store model weights using lower precision.
  2. Perform suitable matrix operations using Tensor Cores.
  3. Accumulate results in a higher-precision format where appropriate.
  4. Apply numerical stability techniques during training.

PyTorch makes this relatively straightforward:

import torch

model = model.cuda()

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
    model.parameters(),
    lr=1e-4
)

for inputs, targets in dataloader:

    inputs = inputs.cuda()
    targets = targets.cuda()

    optimizer.zero_grad()

    with torch.autocast(
        device_type="cuda",
        dtype=torch.bfloat16
    ):
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)

    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

The appropriate precision depends on hardware support, model architecture and numerical stability.

Practical insight: AI engineers should understand precision as a performance, memory and accuracy trade-off, rather than automatically selecting FP32 for every workload.

CUDA: The software layer that makes NVIDIA GPUs programmable

Understanding GPU hardware is only half the story. We also need to understand how software communicates with it.

This is where CUDA comes in.

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA’s parallel computing platform and programming model.

It allows developers to write software that executes computational workloads on NVIDIA GPUs.

Think of CUDA as the bridge between AI frameworks and GPU hardware.

The GPU software stack

A simplified NVIDIA AI software stack looks like this:

Let’s understand the important components.

What happens when you execute a PyTorch operation?

Consider this simple example:

import torch

device = "cuda"

a = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device=device)
b = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device=device)

c = torch.matmul(a, b)

print(c.shape)

What actually happens?

  1. PyTorch creates tensors in GPU memory.
  2. PyTorch dispatches a matrix multiplication operation.
  3. The appropriate backend selects an optimized implementation.
  4. GPU kernels are launched.
  5. The GPU executes matrix operations, potentially using Tensor Cores.
  6. The result is stored in GPU memory.

You wrote just one line of mathematical computation:

c = torch.matmul(a, b)

But underneath, an extensive software and hardware stack is working together.

This abstraction is powerful, but AI engineers should understand what happens beneath it.

Why Triton is becoming important

Traditionally, optimizing GPU kernels required writing CUDA C++.

Triton makes GPU kernel development more accessible through a Python-like programming model.

For example, an engineer can implement a custom matrix operation or fuse multiple operations into one GPU kernel.

Why is kernel fusion important?

Imagine a neural network operation consisting of:

  • Matrix multiplication.
  • Bias addition.
  • Activation function.

A naive implementation may launch three separate kernels and repeatedly read and write intermediate tensors. A fused kernel can perform these operations together, reducing memory traffic and kernel launch overhead. This is particularly valuable in transformer inference and other performance-sensitive AI workloads.

Why GPUs are critical for LLMs: Training versus inference

One of the most useful distinctions for GenAI engineers is understanding how GPU requirements differ between model training and model inference.

Both workloads use GPUs, but their bottlenecks are not identical.

GPU requirements during training

Training a large language model involves:

  1. Forward propagation.
  2. Loss calculation.
  3. Backpropagation.
  4. Gradient computation.
  5. Optimizer updates.

During training, the GPU must store more than model weights. It also needs memory for activations, gradients and optimizer states. Consider a model with 7 billion parameters. A simplified FP16/Adam training memory estimate might look like this:

This is a simplified illustrative estimate, not a complete training-memory budget. Activation memory, temporary buffers, implementation details and checkpointing add further requirements.

This explains why training even a relatively small LLM can require multiple GPUs or memory optimization techniques.

GPU requirements during inference

Inference is different.

The model has already been trained. The GPU executes forward passes to generate predictions or tokens.

For autoregressive LLMs, inference typically consists of two phases:

Phase 1: Prefill

The model processes the input prompt and computes representations for all prompt tokens.

This phase can involve large parallel matrix operations and is often compute-intensive.

Phase 2: Decode

The model generates output tokens one at a time.

At each step, it uses previous context and the KV cache to calculate the next token.

This phase often becomes memory-bandwidth-sensitive, particularly at low batch sizes.

This distinction is extremely important when designing production GenAI infrastructure.

Understanding the KV cache

The Key-Value cache is one of the most important concepts in LLM inference optimization.

In transformer attention, previously computed keys and values can be reused during token generation.

Without caching, the model would repeatedly recompute information for earlier tokens.

With KV caching, the model stores these intermediate representations in GPU memory.

However, the KV cache itself can become very large.

  • L = number of transformer layers.
  • B = batch size.
  • S = sequence length.
  • H_{KV} = number of KV heads.
  • D = head dimension.
  • P = bytes per element.
  • 2 represents Key and Value tensors.

For example, consider:

  • 32 layers.
  • Batch size of 1.
  • 32,768 tokens.
  • 8 KV heads.
  • Head dimension of 128.
  • BF16 precision (2 bytes).

The KV cache requirement is:

That is approximately 2 GiB of KV cache for one sequence.

Now imagine serving 100 concurrent users with the same context length.

The cache requirement could approach 200 GiB, assuming the same architecture and context length for every request.

This is why modern inference engines use techniques such as:

  • PagedAttention.
  • KV cache quantization.
  • Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
  • Continuous batching.
  • Prefix caching.
  • Memory-efficient attention.

These techniques are essential for scaling LLM inference economically.

Multi-GPU computing: How large models use multiple GPUs

What happens when a model cannot fit on one GPU?

The solution is to distribute the workload across multiple GPUs.

However, simply connecting multiple GPUs does not automatically multiply performance.

We need to understand distributed computing strategies.

Data Parallelism

In data parallelism:

  • Each GPU maintains a copy of the model.
  • Different GPUs process different batches of data.
  • Gradients are synchronized between GPUs.

For example:

If you have four GPUs and a global batch size of 256, each GPU may process 64 samples per step.

This is commonly implemented using PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP).

Tensor Parallelism

Tensor parallelism divides individual model operations across GPUs.

For example, a large matrix multiplication can be partitioned so that multiple GPUs calculate different portions of the output.

The results are then combined through communication operations.

This is particularly useful for large transformer models that cannot efficiently fit on a single GPU.

Pipeline Parallelism

Pipeline parallelism divides a neural network into sequential stages.

For example:

  • GPU 1: Transformer layers 1–8.
  • GPU 2: Transformer layers 9–16.
  • GPU 3: Transformer layers 17–24.
  • GPU 4: Transformer layers 25–32.

Microbatches move through these stages, allowing different GPUs to work simultaneously.

NVLink and PCIe: Why interconnects matter

GPUs also need to communicate with each other.

Two important technologies are:

  • PCIe: A general-purpose high-speed interface connecting CPUs, GPUs and other devices.
  • NVLink: NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth interconnect technology for GPU-to-GPU and certain CPU-to-GPU communication.

For large-scale AI workloads, communication overhead can significantly affect training speed.

Imagine four GPUs that spend 30% of their execution time waiting for synchronization.

Even if each GPU is extremely powerful, overall system performance will suffer.

This is why GPU clusters must be designed around both computation and communication.

AMD also has its Infinity Fabric interconnect technology and ROCm software ecosystem, providing an alternative accelerator platform.

Understanding GPU bottlenecks: Compute-bound versus memory-bound workloads

An AI engineer should be able to answer this question:

Is my GPU slow because it cannot compute fast enough, or because it cannot access data fast enough?

These are two different problems.

Compute-bound workloads

A workload is compute-bound when the processor’s mathematical execution capability is the primary limitation.

Examples:

  • Large matrix multiplications.
  • Dense neural network operations.
  • Certain training workloads.

Potential solutions:

  • Use optimized matrix operations.
  • Enable mixed precision.
  • Improve batching.
  • Use Tensor Cores.
  • Optimize kernel execution.

Memory-bound workloads

A workload is memory-bound when data movement limits performance.

Examples:

  • Token-by-token LLM decoding.
  • Operations involving repeated tensor reads and writes.
  • Embedding lookups.
  • Certain attention operations.

Potential solutions:

  • Reduce unnecessary memory transfers.
  • Use kernel fusion.
  • Improve memory access patterns.
  • Quantize model weights.
  • Reuse cached data.
  • Optimize KV cache management.

The Roofline Model

The Roofline Model is a useful performance-analysis framework in high-performance computing.

It relates:

  1. Peak computational performance.
  2. Memory bandwidth.
  3. Arithmetic intensity.

Arithmetic intensity is defined as:

The theoretical performance limit is approximately:

Where:

  • P_{peak} = peak compute capability.
  • BW = memory bandwidth.
  • AI = arithmetic intensity.

The model provides a useful mental framework:

  • Low arithmetic intensity: likely memory-bound.
  • High arithmetic intensity: potentially compute-bound.

The important word is potentially. Real performance also depends on occupancy, instruction efficiency, launch overhead, synchronization and memory access patterns.

This framework helps engineers understand why adding more GPU compute does not always make an AI application faster.

10. GPU optimization techniques every AI engineer should know

Knowing GPU architecture is useful only when you can apply that knowledge to real workloads.

Here are some practical optimization techniques.

Quantization

Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent model parameters.

For example, converting FP16 weights into INT8 or 4-bit representations reduces memory requirements.

A 7-billion-parameter model:

These are raw parameter storage estimates using decimal GB. Actual memory consumption is higher because of metadata, scales, runtime buffers and other overheads.

Popular approaches include:

  • GPTQ.
  • AWQ.
  • bitsandbytes.
  • GGUF-based quantization.

FlashAttention

Traditional attention can require large intermediate memory allocations.

FlashAttention uses an IO-aware algorithm that reduces memory traffic by computing attention in tiles and making better use of on-chip memory.

This makes it especially useful for long sequences.

It is not simply a faster attention implementation; it changes how data moves through the GPU memory hierarchy.

Gradient checkpointing

During training, intermediate activations are required for backpropagation.

Storing every activation can consume significant memory.

Gradient checkpointing trades additional computation for lower memory usage by recomputing selected activations during the backward pass.

This enables training larger models or using larger batch sizes with limited GPU memory.

Batching and continuous batching

Consider an LLM serving 100 users.

If every request is processed independently, GPU utilization may be inefficient.

Batching groups multiple requests into one execution workload.

Continuous batching goes further by dynamically adding and removing requests as sequences finish.

This improves resource utilization and throughput, although it must be balanced against latency requirements.

GPU profiling: How do you know whether your GPU is being utilized properly?

This is where theoretical knowledge becomes practical engineering.

Imagine you deploy a PyTorch model on an NVIDIA A100 or H100. Your application is running, but GPU utilization is only 25%.

Does this mean you need a more powerful GPU?

Not necessarily.

Possible reasons include:

  • CPU bottlenecks.
  • Slow data loading.
  • Frequent CPU-to-GPU transfers.
  • Small batch sizes.
  • Inefficient GPU kernels.
  • Excessive synchronization.
  • Memory bottlenecks.

AI engineers should learn to profile before upgrading hardware.

Essential GPU monitoring tools

Basic GPU monitoring

Start with:
nvidia-smi

For continuous monitoring:
watch -n 1 nvidia-smi

For detailed utilization information:
nvidia-smi dmon

Check GPU information using PyTorch

import torch

if torch.cuda.is_available():

    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

    print(
        "Total memory:",
        torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory / 1e9,
        "GB"
    )

    print(
        "Allocated:",
        torch.cuda.memory_allocated(0) / 1e9,
        "GB"
    )

    print(
        "Reserved:",
        torch.cuda.memory_reserved(0) / 1e9,
        "GB"
    )

else:
    print("CUDA GPU not available")

An important distinction:

  • memory_allocated() measures memory occupied by tensors.
  • memory_reserved() measures memory managed by PyTorch's caching allocator.

Consequently, nvidia-smi may report more memory usage than the memory occupied by live PyTorch tensors.

Benchmarking correctly

One common mistake is benchmarking GPU operations without accounting for asynchronous execution.

CUDA operations are generally asynchronous from the CPU’s perspective.

This means the CPU may continue executing before the GPU finishes its work.

A simple benchmark should synchronize the GPU before measuring elapsed time.

import torch
import time

a = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")
b = torch.randn(4096, 4096, device="cuda")

# Warm-up
for _ in range(10):
    c = torch.matmul(a, b)

torch.cuda.synchronize()

start = time.perf_counter()

for _ in range(100):
    c = torch.matmul(a, b)

torch.cuda.synchronize()

end = time.perf_counter()

print("Average time:", (end - start) / 100)

For serious benchmarking, also control for clock variation, warm-up effects, compilation, memory allocation and competing workloads.

How to choose the right GPU for an AI workload

Not every AI application needs an H100 or a Rubin-class accelerator.

The right GPU depends on the workload, model size, concurrency, latency requirements and budget.

Here is a practical decision framework.

NVIDIA versus AMD

The GPU market is not limited to NVIDIA.

Two major accelerator ecosystems include NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm.

NVIDIA

  • CUDA ecosystem.
  • Tensor Cores.
  • cuDNN and cuBLAS.
  • NCCL.
  • Broad AI framework integration.

AMD

  • ROCm ecosystem.
  • CDNA architecture.
  • Matrix Core technology.
  • RCCL.
  • Large HBM configurations.

The NVIDIA ecosystem has historically had a significant advantage in software maturity and broad developer adoption. AMD has been expanding its accelerator and software capabilities.

For production deployments, evaluate:

  • Framework compatibility.
  • Kernel availability.
  • Model support.
  • Quantization support.
  • Inference engine compatibility.
  • Cluster networking.
  • Cost per generated token.
  • Operational reliability.

Do not select a GPU only because its advertised TFLOPS number is higher.

The next generation of GPU computing: Why AI hardware is evolving

GPU architecture is evolving rapidly because the requirements of AI workloads are changing.

Earlier generations of deep learning workloads focused heavily on matrix multiplication and training throughput.

Modern workloads increasingly include:

  • Long-context LLMs.
  • Multimodal models.
  • Mixture-of-Experts architectures.
  • Reasoning models.
  • Agentic AI systems.
  • Video generation.
  • Real-time inference.

These workloads introduce new requirements for memory capacity, memory bandwidth, communication and energy efficiency.

NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin

NVIDIA’s Blackwell generation introduced major advancements in AI compute, memory systems and multi-GPU architecture.

Why this matters for agentic AI

Think about a modern AI agent.

Unlike a traditional LLM request, an agent may:

  1. Receive a user request.
  2. Reason about the problem.
  3. Search external information.
  4. Call tools.
  5. Read results.
  6. Reconsider its approach.
  7. Generate another response.
  8. Repeat until the task is completed.

A complex agentic workflow can involve many sequential inference calls, long context windows and concurrent execution. This changes the economics of AI infrastructure. The important metrics are no longer just training FLOPS.

They increasingly include:

  • Tokens per second.
  • Time to first token (TTFT).
  • Inter-token latency.
  • Concurrent requests.
  • KV cache capacity.
  • Energy per token.
  • Cost per successful task.

For agentic AI, GPU infrastructure must support sustained inference and high concurrency efficiently.

This is why memory bandwidth and capacity are becoming increasingly important alongside raw compute performance.

Final thoughts: GPUs are becoming an essential part of AI engineering

The evolution of AI is not just about bigger models, more parameters or better algorithms.

It is also about how efficiently we execute those algorithms on increasingly sophisticated hardware.

As AI engineers, we often spend considerable time thinking about model architectures, embeddings, RAG pipelines, fine-tuning and agentic workflows.

But production AI performance is determined by the interaction between software and hardware.

Understanding GPUs helps answer some of the most important engineering questions:

  • Why does my LLM require so much GPU memory?
  • Why is inference slower despite having a powerful GPU?
  • Why does BF16 outperform FP32 for certain workloads?
  • Why does increasing batch size improve throughput?
  • Why is token generation often memory-bound?
  • Why do some models require multiple GPUs?
  • How can I reduce inference costs without compromising quality?

The next generation of AI engineers will need to understand not only how to build intelligent models, but also how to execute them efficiently.

The real competitive advantage is not simply having access to powerful GPUs. It is knowing how to extract maximum performance from them.
